payload.name: Zeigarnik effect
payload.fact: The unfinishedness of events is spontaneously extracted and prioritized in visual processing, leading to more precise memory for unfinished visual paths compared to completed ones.
payload.boundary: The effect is not universal and its replicability has been challenged, with some studies finding that completed tasks are sometimes recalled more frequently.

provenance.quote_or_locus: subjects remembered items they had failed to complete almost twice as often as those they had solved

provenance.title: The “unfinishedness” of dynamic events is spontaneously extracted in visual processing: A new ‘Visual Zeigarnik Effect’
provenance.quote_or_locus: Although this manipulation was entirely task-irrelevant, it nevertheless had a powerful influence on visual memory: observers placed probes much closer to their correct locations on Unfinished trials

provenance.title: The interruption of tasks: Methodological, factual, and theoretical issues.
provenance.quote_or_locus: In the first place, the Zeigarnik effect is far from being the invariable result in ITP. Frequently, more completed than incompleted tasks are recalled

provenance.title: The interruption of tasks: Methodological, factual, and theoretical issues.
provenance.quote_or_locus: Zeigarnik (1927) first introduced ITP as a test of the prediction from the gestalt theory of motivation that interrupted tasks should be recalled more frequently than completed tasks. Her findings supported this prediction and is known to this day as the Zeigarnik effect
